title: Given a binary tree, find its diameter, defined as the number of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. The path may or may not pass through the root. Explain why a single post-order traversal that returns subtree heights while updating a global maximum is the efficient solution.
shortTitle: Tree Diameter (Longest Path Between Any Two Nodes)
keyPoints: The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes; this version counts in nodes (leftHeight + rightHeight + 1)
A single post-order traversal returns height and updates the maximum diameter simultaneously
The candidate diameter through any node is leftHeight + rightHeight + 1 (counting nodes)
The path may not pass through the root, so every node must be evaluated as a potential turning point
The naive approach recomputes heights at every node and is O(n^2); the fused approach is O(n)
The counting convention (nodes vs edges) must be stated explicitly to avoid off-by-one errors

s1_definition.oneliner: Post-order return each subtree's height, and at every node update the best diameter as left height plus right height plus one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Diameter (in nodes)** – the number of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes in the tree.
- **Key insight** – the longest path through any node is `leftHeight + rightHeight + 1` (the left depth, plus the node itself, plus the right depth).
- **Efficient approach** – a single post-order traversal returns height while updating a shared maximum.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(h) space.
- **Convention** – in nodes: `leftHeight + rightHeight + 1`; in edges: `leftHeight + rightHeight`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy is a tree. Management wants the longest possible escalation path between any two desks, measured in number of desks visited. That longest stretch might not go through the head office at all; it could run up one branch and down another. At every desk, the span is how deep the left reports go plus one (the desk itself) plus how deep the right reports go.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Post-Order Diameter (Nodes)

         CEO         height=3
        /   \        diameter through CEO: 3+2+1=6
      VP1   VP2      height=2, height=2
      /       \
    DIR1     DIR2    height=1, height=1
    /
  MGR1               height=1

  maxDiameter: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 6
  Answer: 6 nodes
  Path: MGR1 → DIR1 → VP1 → CEO → VP2 → DIR2
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The tree diameter counted in nodes is the longest path between any two nodes, measured by how many nodes it visits. The key insight is that the longest path through any node equals leftHeight + rightHeight + 1 (left depth, the node itself, right depth). A single post-order traversal returns each subtree's height while updating a shared maximum with this candidate, keeping the algorithm linear.

The naive approach recomputes heights at every node and degrades to quadratic on skewed trees. The fused approach computes each node's height exactly once. This pattern of returning one value while updating a global with another is reusable across diameter (edges), diameter (nodes), and maximum path sum problems.

Always state the counting convention. Node-counted diameter uses `left + right + 1`; edge-counted uses `left + right`. A single node has diameter 1 in nodes and 0 in edges. Confusing the two is the most common mistake.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, this measures the longest escalation chain in the org hierarchy. An over-long chain slows approvals, so the diameter is tracked as a health metric. The path often runs between two deep branches through a mid-level manager rather than through the CEO.

Remember one sentence: fuse height and diameter in post-order; `leftHeight + rightHeight + 1` at each node is the candidate diameter in nodes.
